steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper proposing a training paradigm that uses a multilingual language model as a pivot so large multimodal models can work in non-English languages using only English image-text data. Cover the motivation, the method idea, the Chinese and multilingual models we built, and our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Rise of large multimodal models (image-to-text, text-to-image)
- Problem: multimodal success mostly in English; non-English data scarce
- MpM: multilingual model as pivot, inspired by Bilingual Dual-coding Theory
- Two stages: multilingual alignment, multimodal alignment
- Instantiation: VisCPM for Chinese; six-language extension
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Rise of large multimodal models
  - GPT-4 (cite), Stable Diffusion: rapid advances in multimodal capability; latest frontier toward AGI
  - (i) image-to-text: multimodal LLMs GPT-4 (cite), LLaVA (cite), InstructBLIP (cite): conversation and reasoning on images
  - (ii) text-to-image: Imagen, Stable Diffusion: realistic, relevant images from text prompts
  - reshaping multimodal AI in academia and industry
- Problem
  - success mainly in English community; other languages trail behind
  - hard to bridge: training needs lots of image-text pairs
  - BLIP-2 (cite) pretraining: more than 100M high-quality pairs; Stable Diffusion: more than 2B
  - paucity of multimodal data in non-English languages -> progress hindered
- MpM
  - training paradigm for large multimodal models in non-English languages
  - Multilingual language model to Pivot Multimodal learning; English (lots of multimodal data) as pivot between visual signals and non-English languages
  - inspired by Bilingual Dual-coding Theory (cite, two): visual semantics largely language-agnostic
  - Fig. 1(a): multilingual learners align visual semantics with newly acquired language via existing multimodal + multilingual alignment
  - two consecutive stages: multilingual alignment -> multilingual model; multimodal alignment -> multimodal model spanning languages
- Two stages in detail
  - multilingual alignment: pretrained multilingual LLM as backbone, aligned representations across languages
  - multimodal alignment: train visual modules on the multilingual model only on English image-text pairs
  - multilingual model as pivot -> zero-shot multimodal capability in other languages, like humans
- Instantiation
  - Chinese: VisCPM, based on English-Chinese bilingual LLM CPM-Bee
  - pretraining only on English pairs, zero-shot Chinese performance beats Chinese multimodal models trained on native Chinese pairs
  - potential for broader languages
  - same process with LLaMA: multilingual multimodal conversation model, six languages: English, German, French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese
- Contributions
  - (i) MpM for non-English languages lacking multimodal resources; researchers can rapidly adapt English methods
  - (ii) VisCPM series, state-of-the-art among open-source Chinese multimodal models
  - (iii) open-source VisCPM weights + experimental details
  - (iv) validate generalization to diverse languages; six-language conversation model

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Powerful models like GPT-4 and Stable Diffusion are advancing rapidly in their multimodal capabilities, and large multimodal models have become the latest frontier in the pursuit of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI). In general, multimodal generative capabilities over images and text fall into two categories. (i) In image-to-text generation, multimodal large language models like GPT-4, LLaVA and InstructBLIP show remarkable abilities for multimodal conversation and reasoning based on images. (ii) In text-to-image generation, models like Imagen and Stable Diffusion are very good at generating realistic and relevant images from text prompts. These models are exceptionally good at processing images and text, and they are deeply reshaping multimodal AI in both academia and industry.

But the success of large multimodal models has mostly happened in the English community, and the multimodal capabilities in other non-English languages are far behind. It is hard to close this gap because training multimodal models requires a lot of image-text pair data. For example, pretraining BLIP-2 uses more than 100M high-quality image-text pairs, and Stable Diffusion uses more than 2B pairs. Since there are so few multimodal data resources like this in non-English languages, multimodal research in these languages is held back.

- MpM: training paradigm for large multimodal models in non-English languages
  - Multilingual language model to Pivot Multimodal learning; English as pivot between visual signals and non-English languages
  - inspired by Bilingual Dual-coding Theory: visual semantics largely language-agnostic; Fig. 1(a) multilingual learners
  - two consecutive stages: multilingual alignment (multilingual model), multimodal alignment (multimodal model across languages)
- Stages: pretrained multilingual LLM backbone with aligned representations; visual modules trained only on English image-text pairs; pivot -> zero-shot capability in other languages
- VisCPM for Chinese on CPM-Bee; English-only pretraining still beats native-Chinese-trained models zero-shot; LLaMA-based six-language conversation model (English, German, French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese)
- Contributions (i)-(iv): MpM; VisCPM state-of-the-art among open-source Chinese models; open-source weights and details; generalization, six-language model

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Powerful models like GPT-4 and Stable Diffusion are advancing rapidly in their multimodal capabilities, and large multimodal models have become the latest frontier in the pursuit of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI). In general, multimodal generative capabilities over images and text fall into two categories. (i) In image-to-text generation, multimodal large language models like GPT-4, LLaVA and InstructBLIP show remarkable abilities for multimodal conversation and reasoning based on images. (ii) In text-to-image generation, models like Imagen and Stable Diffusion are very good at generating realistic and relevant images from text prompts. These models are exceptionally good at processing images and text, and they are deeply reshaping multimodal AI in both academia and industry.

But the success of large multimodal models has mostly happened in the English community, and the multimodal capabilities in other non-English languages are far behind. It is hard to close this gap because training multimodal models requires a lot of image-text pair data. For example, pretraining BLIP-2 uses more than 100M high-quality image-text pairs, and Stable Diffusion uses more than 2B pairs. Since there are so few multimodal data resources like this in non-English languages, multimodal research in these languages is held back.

To deal with this problem we propose MpM, which is an effective training paradigm for large multimodal models in non-English languages. MpM uses the Multilingual language model to Pivot Multimodal learning across languages. It treats English, which has lots of multimodal data resources, as a pivot between the visual signals and the non-English languages that usually lack multimodal data. MpM is inspired by the Bilingual Dual-coding Theory, which argues that visual semantics are mostly language-agnostic. Intuitively, as shown in Fig. 1(a), multilingual learners can align visual semantics with a newly learned language based on the multimodal and multilingual alignment they already have. MpM simulates this human learning process and splits non-English multimodal learning into two consecutive stages, multilingual alignment and multimodal alignment. The first stage builds a multilingual model, and the second stage ends up with a multimodal model that covers multiple languages.

For multilingual alignment, MpM uses a pretrained multilingual large language model (LLM) as the backbone language model, and this model gives aligned representations for different languages. Then for multimodal alignment, MpM trains the visual modules on top of the multilingual model using only English image-text pairs, so that English and visual semantics are aligned. Like in human learning, the multilingual model works as a pivot, and the resulting multimodal model naturally gets zero-shot multimodal capability in the other non-English languages.

We take Chinese as a practical example of MpM and develop Chinese large multimodal models called VisCPM, based on the English-Chinese bilingual large language model CPM-Bee. Even though it is pretrained only on English image-text pairs, VisCPM's zero-shot performance in Chinese is better than existing Chinese multimodal models that were trained on image-text pairs in native Chinese. This promising performance in Chinese suggests MpM could be applied to more languages. Using the same training process, we also extend MpM to build a multilingual multimodal conversation model based on LLaMA that supports six languages: English, German, French, Spanish, Italian, and Portuguese.

To sum up, the contributions of this paper are: (i) We propose MpM, an effective training paradigm designed for non-English languages that lack multimodal resources. Researchers around the world can use MpM to quickly adapt advanced multimodal learning methods from English to their own languages. (ii) We develop a series of Chinese large multimodal models, VisCPM, as a practical application of MpM, and it achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source Chinese multimodal models. (iii) We open-source the model weights of VisCPM and give experimental details, which can be a useful reference for other researchers. (iv) We validate that VisCPM generalizes to diverse languages and develop the multilingual multimodal conversation model for six languages.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
With the rapid advancement of powerful models such as GPT-4 [1] and Stable Diffusion in their multimodal capabilities, large multimodal models have emerged as the latest frontier in pursuing Artificial General Intelligence (AGI). Generally, the multimodal generative capabilities across images and text can be divided into two categories: (i) In image-to-text generation, prominent multimodal large language models like GPT-4 [1], LLaVA [2] and InstructBLIP [3] exhibit remarkable multimodal conversational and reasoning abilities based on images; (ii) In text-to-image generation, models such as Imagen and Stable Diffusion excel at generating highly realistic and relevant images from text prompts. These models have exceptional capabilities in processing images and text, profoundly reshaping multimodal AI in both academia and industry.

However, the success of large multimodal models has mainly been achieved within the English community, while multimodal capabilities in non-English languages significantly trail behind. Bridging this gap is challenging because training multimodal models requires extensive image-text pair data. For instance, the pretraining of BLIP-2 [4] involves more than 100M high-quality image-text pairs, while Stable Diffusion uses more than 2B pairs. Because of the paucity of such multimodal data resources in non-English languages, the progress of multimodal research in these languages remains hindered.

To address this challenge, we propose MpM, an effective training paradigm for large multimodal models in non-English languages. MpM uses the Multilingual language model to Pivot Multimodal learning across languages, and considers English, which contains substantial multimodal data resources, as a pivot between the visual signals and non-English languages, which commonly lack multimodal data. MpM draws inspiration from the Bilingual Dual-coding Theory [5,6], which argues that visual semantics are largely language-agnostic. Intuitively, as portrayed in Fig. 1(a), multilingual learners can effectively align visual semantics with a newly acquired language based on established multimodal and multilingual alignment. Simulating the human learning process, MpM divides non-English multimodal learning into two consecutive stages: multilingual alignment and multimodal alignment. The former focuses on building a multilingual model, while the latter culminates in a multimodal model spanning multiple languages.

Specifically, for multilingual alignment, MpM uses a pretrained multilingual large language model (LLM) as the backbone language model, which provides aligned representations for different languages. Next, for multimodal alignment, MpM trains the visual modules based on the multilingual model exclusively on English image-text pairs to align English and visual semantics. Similar to how humans learn, with the multilingual model as a pivot point, the resulting multimodal model naturally acquires zero-shot multimodal capability in other non-English languages.

Taking Chinese as a practical instance of MpM, we develop Chinese large multimodal models named VisCPM based on the English-Chinese bilingual large language model CPM-Bee. Notably, although pretrained exclusively on English image-text pairs, VisCPM's zero-shot performance in Chinese still surpasses that of existing Chinese multimodal models trained on native Chinese image-text pairs. This promising performance in Chinese suggests MpM's potential for broader languages. Following the same training process, we further extend MpM to develop a multilingual multimodal conversation model based on LLaMA supporting six languages, including English, German, French, Spanish, Italian, and Portuguese.

In summary, the contributions of this paper are as follows: (i) We propose MpM, an effective training paradigm designed for non-English languages lacking multimodal resources. Researchers worldwide can use MpM to rapidly adapt advanced multimodal learning methods from English to their own languages. (ii) We develop a series of Chinese large multimodal models, VisCPM, as a practical application of MpM, which achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source Chinese multimodal models. (iii) We open-source the model weights of VisCPM and provide experimental details as a valuable reference for other researchers. (iv) We validate the generalization capability of VisCPM in diverse languages and develop a multilingual multimodal conversation model across six languages.
